content.question_text: What is an interface in Java?

core_requirements: An interface is a reference type that defines a contract — it tells classes what to do but not how.
It contains abstract method signatures that implementing classes must provide.
acceptable_variations: A technique of telling classes what to do but not how.
A set of requirements that a class must fulfill.

core_requirements: No — an interface is not a class.
It is a reference type that defines a set of abstract methods.
acceptable_variations: No, it's a set of requirements.

content.question_text: What is the default access modifier given to methods in an interface?

core_requirements: public — all interface methods are implicitly public abstract.
Interfaces cannot have instance fields (they can only have static final constants).
They cannot have constructors or state.

content.question_text: Which keyword is used to implement an interface in Java?

core_requirements: implements

content.question_text: Write an example of how to implement an interface.

core_requirements: Syntax: class ClassName implements InterfaceName { }
Example: class Example implements Comparable { }

content.question_text: What is required of a class after it implements an interface?

core_requirements: It must provide concrete implementations for all abstract methods declared in the interface.
If it doesn't, the class must be declared abstract.
acceptable_variations: It must implement all methods of the interface.
Provide implementations for all interface methods.

content.question_text: Are methods implemented by a class for an interface also public by default?

core_requirements: No — the implementing class methods must be explicitly declared public.
If you use a more restrictive access modifier, the compiler will complain.
acceptable_variations: No, they need the public modifier.

content.question_text: What happens if you don't use a generic type when implementing an interface?

core_requirements: You use a raw type, which is treated as an Object type.
This requires explicit casting when accessing the elements.
acceptable_variations: It becomes a raw type of Object, requiring casts.

content.question_text: Should the compareTo method be compatible with the equals method? If yes, how?

core_requirements: Yes — if x.equals(y) returns true, then x.compareTo(y) should return 0.
This is recommended for consistency, though not strictly required.
acceptable_variations: Yes, x.compareTo(y) should return 0 if x.equals(y) is true.

content.question_text: What are the possible return values of the compareTo() method?

core_requirements: A positive integer (e.g., 1) if the first object is greater than the second.
A negative integer (e.g., -1) if the first object is less than the second.
Zero (0) if the two objects are equal.

content.question_text: What is required in subclasses when the notion of comparison is different?

core_requirements: You should outlaw comparison of objects that belong to different classes.
This prevents comparing incompatible types.

content.question_text: How do you outlaw comparison of objects that belong to different classes in code?

core_requirements: Check: if (getClass() != other.getClass()) throw new ClassCastException();
This ensures only objects of the same class can be compared.

content.question_text: What is required in subclasses when the notion of comparison is fixed?

core_requirements: Supply a simple compareTo method in the superclass and make it final.
This ensures the comparison behavior is consistent across all subclasses.
acceptable_variations: Make the compareTo method final in the superclass.
